قَوْلُهُ تَعَالَى: ﴿وَحِيلَ بَيْنَهُمْ وَبَيْنَ مَا يَشْتَهُونَ﴾ قِيلَ: ﴿حِيلَ بَيْنَهُمْ وَبَيْنَ النَّجَاةِ مِنَ الْعَذَابِ﴾. وَقِيلَ: ﴿حِيلَ بَيْنَهُمْ وَبَيْنَ مَا يَشْتَهُونَ فِي الدُّنْيَا مِنْ أَمْوَالِهِمْ وَأَهْلِيهِمْ﴾. وَمَذْهَبُ قَتَادَةَ (Qatadah) أَنَّ الْمَعْنَى أَنَّهُمْ كَانُوا يَشْتَهُونَ لَمَّا رَأَوُا الْعَذَابَ أَنْ يُقْبَلَ مِنْهُمْ أَنْ يُطِيعُوا اللَّهَ عز وجل وَيَنْتَهُوا إِلَى مَا يَأْمُرُهُمْ بِهِ اللَّهُ، فَحِيلَ بَيْنَهُمْ وَبَيْنَ ذَلِكَ، لِأَنَّ ذَلِكَ إِنَّمَا كَانَ فِي الدُّنْيَا أَوْ قَدْ زَالَتْ فِي ذَلِكَ الْوَقْتِ. وَالْأَصْلُ "حُوِلَ"، فَقُلِبَتْ حَرَكَةُ الْوَاوِ عَلَى الْحَاءِ فَانْقَلَبَتْ يَاءً، ثُمَّ حُذِفَتْ حَرَكَتُهَا لِثِقَلِهَا.

(كَما فُعِلَ بِأَشْياعِهِمْ) الْأَشْيَاعُ جَمْعُ شَيْعٍ، وَشِيَعٌ جَمْعُ شِيعَةٍ.

(مِنْ قَبْلُ) أَيْ بِمَنْ مَضَى مِنَ الْقُرُونِ السَّالِفَةِ الْكَافِرَةِ.

(إِنَّهُمْ كانُوا فِي شَكٍّ) أَيْ مِنْ أَمْرِ الرُّسُلِ وَالْبَعْثِ وَالْجَنَّةِ وَالنَّارِ. وَقِيلَ: فِي الدِّينِ وَالتَّوْحِيدِ، وَالْمَعْنَى وَاحِدٌ.

(مُرِيبٍ) أَيْ يُسْتَرَابُ بِهِ، يُقَالُ: أَرَابَ الرَّجُلُ أَيْ صَارَ ذَا رِيبَةٍ، فَهُوَ مُرِيبٌ. وَمَنْ قَالَ هُوَ مِنَ الرَّيْبِ الَّذِي هُوَ الشَّكُّ وَالتُّهْمَةُ قَالَ: يُقَالُ شَكٌّ مُرِيبٌ، كَمَا يُقَالُ: عَجَبٌ عَجِيبٌ وَشِعْرُ شَاعِرٍ، فِي التَّأْكِيدِ. خُتِمَتِ السُّورَةُ، وَالْحَمْدُ لله رب العالمين.

[سورة فاطر]

بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمنِ الرَّحِيمِ. سورة فاطر مكية في قول الجميع، وهي خمس وأربعون آية.

بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمنِ الرَّحِيمِ

﴿الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ فاطِرِ السَّماواتِ وَالْأَرْضِ جاعِلِ الْمَلائِكَةِ رُسُلاً أُولِي أَجْنِحَةٍ مَثْنى وَثُلاثَ وَرُباعَ يَزِيدُ فِي الْخَلْقِ مَا يَشاءُ إِنَّ اللَّهَ عَلى كُلِّ شَيْءٍ قَدِيرٌ﴾ (١)

قَوْلُهُ تَعَالَى: ﴿الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ فاطِرِ السَّماواتِ وَالْأَرْضِ﴾. يَجُوزُ فِي "فاطِرِ" ثَلَاثَةُ أَوْجُهٍ: الْخَفْضُ عَلَى النَّعْتِ (al-na't, the adjectival qualifier)، وَالرَّفْعُ عَلَى إِضْمَارِ مُبْتَدَأٍ، وَالنَّصْبُ عَلَى الْمَدْحِ. وَحَكَى سِيبَوَيْهِ (Sibawayh): الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ أَهْلُ الْحَمْدِ [مِثْلُهُ [زيادة عن كتاب النحاس يقتضيها السياق.]]، وَكَذَا "جاعِلِ الْمَلائِكَةِ". وَالْفَاطِرُ: الْخَالِقُ. وَقَدْ مَضَى فِي "يُوسُفَ" [راجع ج ٩ ص ٢٧٩ ج ٦ ص (٣٩٧)] وَغَيْرِهَا. وَالْفَطْرُ: الشَّقُّ عَنِ الشَّيْءِ، يُقَالُ: فَطَرْتُهُ فَانْفَطَرَ. وَمِنْهُ: فَطَرَ نَابُ الْبَعِيرِ طَلَعَ، فَهُوَ بَعِيرٌ فَاطِرٌ. وَتَفَطَّرَ الشَّيْءُ تَشَقَّقَ. وَسَيْفٌ فُطَارٌ، أَيْ فِيهِ تَشَقُّقٌ. قَالَ عَنْتَرَةُ:

وَسَيْفِي كَالْعَقِيقَةِ فَهْوَ كِمْعِي ... سِلَاحِي لَا أَفَلَّ وَلَا فُطَارَا [عقيقة البرق: شعاعه. والكمع (بكسر فسكون) والكميع: الضجيع.]

وَالْفَطْرُ: الِابْتِدَاءُ وَالِاخْتِرَاعُ. قَالَ ابْنُ عَبَّاسٍ (Ibn Abbas): كُنْتُ لَا أَدْرِي مَا "فاطِرِ السَّماواتِ وَالْأَرْضِ" حَتَّى أَتَانِي أَعْرَابِيَّانِ يَخْتَصِمَانِ فِي بِئْرٍ، فَقَالَ أَحَدُهُمَا: أَنَا فَطَرْتُهَا، أَيْ أَنَا ابْتَدَأْتُهَا. وَالْفَطْرُ: حَلْبُ النَّاقَةِ بِالسَّبَّابَةِ وَالْإِبْهَامِ. وَالْمُرَادُ بِذِكْرِ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ الْعَالَمُ كُلُّهُ، وَنَبَّهَ بِهَذَا عَلَى أَنَّ مَنْ قَدَرَ عَلَى الِابْتِدَاءِ قَادِرٌ عَلَى الْإِعَادَةِ. "جاعِلِ الْمَلائِكَةِ" لَا يَجُوزُ فِيهِ التَّنْوِينُ (tanwin, nunation)، لِأَنَّهُ لِمَا مَضَى. "رُسُلًا" مَفْعُولٌ ثَانٍ، وَيُقَالُ: عَلَى إِضْمَارِ فِعْلٍ، لِأَنَّ "فَاعِلًا" إِذَا كَانَ لِمَا مَضَى لَمْ يَعْمَلْ فِيهِ شَيْئًا، وَإِعْمَالُهُ عَلَى أَنَّهُ مُسْتَقْبَلٌ حُذِفَ التَّنْوِينُ مِنْهُ تَخْفِيفًا. وَقَرَأَ الضَّحَّاكُ: "الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ فَطَرَ السماوات والأرض" عَلَى الْفِعْلِ الْمَاضِي.

(جاعِلِ الْمَلائِكَةِ رُسُلًا) الرُّسُلُ مِنْهُمْ جِبْرِيلُ وَمِيكَائِيلُ وَإِسْرَافِيلُ وَمَلَكُ الْمَوْتِ، صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِمْ أَجْمَعِينَ. وَقَرَأَ الْحَسَنُ: "جَاعِلُ الْمَلَائِكَةِ" بِالرَّفْعِ. وَقَرَأَ خُلَيْدُ بْنُ نَشِيطٍ: "جَعَلَ الْمَلَائِكَةَ"، وَكُلُّهُ ظَاهِرٌ.

(أُولِي أَجْنِحَةٍ) نَعْتٌ، أَيْ أَصْحَابُ أَجْنِحَةٍ.

(مَثْنى وَثُلاثَ وَرُباعَ) [في كتاب البحر: وقيل (أُولِي أَجْنِحَةٍ) معترض، و(مَثْنى) حال والعامل فعل محذوف يدل عليه (رُسُلًا)، أي يرسلون مثنى وثلاث ورباع.] أَيِ اثْنَيْنِ اثْنَيْنِ، وَثَلَاثَةً ثَلَاثَةً، وَأَرْبَعَةً أَرْبَعَةً. قَالَ قَتَادَةُ: بَعْضُهُمْ لَهُ جَنَاحَانِ، وَبَعْضُهُمْ ثَلَاثَةٌ، وَبَعْضُهُمْ أَرْبَعَةٌ، يَنْزِلُونَ بِهِمَا مِنَ السَّمَاءِ إِلَى الْأَرْضِ، وَيَعْرُجُونَ مِنَ الْأَرْضِ إِلَى السَّمَاءِ، وَهِيَ مَسِيرَةُ كَذَا فِي وَقْتٍ وَاحِدٍ، أَيْ جَعَلَهُمْ رُسُلًا. قَالَ يَحْيَى بْنُ سَلَّامٍ: إِلَى الْأَنْبِيَاءِ. وَقَالَ السُّدِّيُّ: إِلَى الْعِبَادِ بِرَحْمَةٍ أَوْ نِقْمَةٍ. وَفِي صَحِيحِ مُسْلِمٍ عَنِ ابْنِ مَسْعُودٍ أَنَّ النَّبِيَّ ﷺ رَأَى جِبْرِيلَ عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ لَهُ سِتُّمِائَةِ جَنَاحٍ. وَعَنِ الزُّهْرِيِّ أَنَّ جِبْرِيلَ عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ قَالَ لَهُ: (يَا مُحَمَّدُ، لَوْ رَأَيْتَ إِسْرَافِيلَ إِنَّ لَهُ لَاثْنَيْ عَشَرَ أَلْفَ جَنَاحٍ، مِنْهَا جَنَاحٌ بِالْمَشْرِقِ وَجَنَاحٌ بِالْمَغْرِبِ، وَإِنَّ الْعَرْشَ لَعَلَى كَاهِلِهِ، وَإِنَّهُ فِي الْأَحَايِينِ لَيَتَضَاءَلُ لِعَظَمَةِ اللَّهِ حَتَّى يَعُودَ مِثْلَ الْوَصْعِ، وَالْوَصْعُ عُصْفُورٌ صَغِيرٌ، حَتَّى مَا يَحْمِلُ عَرْشَ رَبِّكَ إِلَّا عَظَمَتُهُ). وَ"أُولُو" اسْمُ جَمْعٍ لِـ"ذُو"، كَمَا أَنَّ "هَؤُلَاءِ" اسْمُ جَمْعٍ لِـ"ذَا"، وَنَظِيرُهُمَا فِي الْمُتَمَكِّنَةِ: الْمَخَاضُ [المخاض: الحوامل من النوق، واحدتها خلقة على غير قياس ولا واحد لها من لفظها، كما قالوا لواحدة النساء: امرأة، ولواحدة الإبل: ناقة أو بعير.] وَالْخَلِفَةُ. وَقَدْ مَضَى الْكَلَامُ فِي "مَثْنَى وَثُلَاثَ وَرُبَاعَ" فِي "النِّسَاءِ" [راجع ج ٥ ص ١٥ فما بعد.] وَأَنَّهُ غَيْرُ مُنْصَرِفٍ.

(يَزِيدُ فِي الْخَلْقِ مَا يَشاءُ) أَيْ فِي خَلْقِ الْمَلَائِكَةِ، فِي قَوْلِ أَكْثَرِ الْمُفَسِّرِينَ، ذَكَرَهُ الْمَهْدَوِيُّ. وَقَالَ الْحَسَنُ: "يَزِيدُ فِي الْخَلْقِ" أَيْ فِي أَجْنِحَةِ الْمَلَائِكَةِ مَا يَشَاءُ. وَقَالَ الزُّهْرِيُّ وَابْنُ جُرَيْجٍ: يَعْنِي حُسْنَ الصَّوْتِ. وَقَدْ مَضَى الْقَوْلُ فِيهِ فِي مُقَدِّمَةِ الْكِتَابِ [راجع (باب كيفية التلاوة ولكتاب الله تعالى).]. وَقَالَ الْهَيْثَمُ الْفَارِسِيُّ: رَأَيْتُ النَّبِيَّ ﷺ فِي مَنَامِي، فَقَالَ: (أَنْتَ الْهَيْثَمُ الَّذِي تُزَيِّنُ الْقُرْآنَ بِصَوْتِكَ، جَزَاكَ اللَّهُ خَيْرًا). وَقَالَ قَتَادَةُ: "يَزِيدُ فِي الْخَلْقِ مَا يَشاءُ" الْمَلَاحَةُ فِي الْعَيْنَيْنِ وَالْحُسْنُ فِي الْأَنْفِ وَالْحَلَاوَةُ فِي الْفَمِ. وَقِيلَ: الْخَطُّ الْحَسَنُ. وَقَالَ مُهَاجِرٌ الْكَلَاعِيُّ: قَالَ النَّبِيُّ ﷺ: (الْخَطُّ الْحَسَنُ يَزِيدُ الْكَلَامَ وُضُوحًا). وَقِيلَ: الْوَجْهُ الْحَسَنُ. وَقِيلَ فِي الْخَبَرِ فِي هَذِهِ الْآيَةِ: هُوَ الْوَجْهُ الْحَسَنُ وَالصَّوْتُ الْحَسَنُ وَالشَّعْرُ الْحَسَنُ، ذَكَرَهُ الْقُشَيْرِيُّ. النَّقَّاشُ: هُوَ الشَّعْرُ الْجَعْدُ [ما فيه التواء وتقبض، أو القصير منه.]. وَقِيلَ: الْعَقْلُ وَالتَّمْيِيزُ. وَقِيلَ: الْعُلُومُ وَالصَّنَائِعُ.

(إِنَّ اللَّهَ عَلى كُلِّ شَيْءٍ قَدِيرٌ) مِنَ النُّقْصَانِ وَالزِّيَادَةِ. الزَّمَخْشَرِيُّ: وَالْآيَةُ مُطْلَقَةٌ تَتَنَاوَلُ كُلَّ زِيَادَةٍ فِي الْخَلْقِ، مِنْ طُولِ قَامَةٍ، وَاعْتِدَالِ صُورَةٍ، وَتَمَامٍ فِي الْأَعْضَاءِ، وَقُوَّةٍ فِي الْبَطْشِ، وَحَصَافَةٍ فِي الْعَقْلِ، وَجَزَالَةٍ فِي الرَّأْيِ، وَجُرْأَةٍ فِي الْقَلْبِ، وَسَمَاحَةٍ فِي النَّفْسِ، وَذَلَاقَةٍ فِي اللِّسَانِ، وَلَبَاقَةٍ فِي التَّكَلُّمِ، وَحُسْنِ تَأَتٍّ [تأتّى فلان لحاجته: إذا ترفّق لها وأتاها من وجهها.] فِي مُزَاوَلَةِ الْأُمُورِ، وَمَا أَشْبَهَ ذَلِكَ مِمَّا لَا يُحِيطُ بِهِ وَصْفٌ.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 35, verse 2:

The grammarians permitted, outside of the Qur'an, "فَلَا مُمْسِكَ لَهُ" (fa-la mumsika lahu, "there is none to withhold it"), with agreement to the wording of "مَا" (ma), and "لَها" (laha, "for it") with agreement to the meaning. They also permitted "وَمَا يُمْسِكُ فَلَا مُرْسِلَ لَهَا" (wa-ma yumsik fa-la mursila laha, "and whatever He withholds, there is none to release it after Him"), and they permitted "مَا يَفْتَحُ اللَّهُ لِلنَّاسِ مِنْ رَحْمَةٍ" (ma yaftahu Allahu lil-nasi min rahmatin, "whatever mercy Allah opens for mankind") with the nominative (bil-raf'), in which case "مَا" (ma) carries the sense of "الَّذِي" (alladhi, "that which"), meaning that the messengers were sent as a mercy to mankind, so none other than Allah can send them. It was also said: it refers to what Allah brings to them of rain or provision, so no one can withhold it, and whatever He withholds of that, no one can release it. It was also said: it is supplication; this was said by al-Dahhak. Ibn Abbas said: it is repentance. It was also said: it is success (tawfiq) and guidance (hidayah).

I say: the word "الرَّحْمَةِ" (al-rahmah, "mercy") encompasses all of that, since it is indefinite (munakkarah) for generality and vagueness, so it applies to every mercy by way of substitution (al-badal), and thus it is general in all that has been mentioned.

In the Muwatta' of Malik: it reached him that Abu Hurayrah used to say, when he rose in the morning and people had been given rain: "We have been given rain by the star of al-Fath (nawʾ al-fath)," and then he would recite this verse: "مَا يَفْتَحِ اللَّهُ لِلنَّاسِ مِنْ رَحْمَةٍ فَلا مُمْسِكَ لَها" (ma yaftahi Allahu lil-nasi min rahmatin fa-la mumsika laha, "whatever mercy Allah opens for mankind, none can withhold it").

﴿وَهُوَ الْعَزِيزُ الْحَكِيمُ﴾ ("And He is the Almighty, the Wise"). This has already been mentioned [see vol. 2, p. 131].

Al-Qurtubi's commentary on Surah 35, verse 3:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O mankind, remember the favour of God upon you.﴾ The meaning of this remembrance (dhikr) is gratitude (shukr).

﴿Is there any creator other than God?﴾ The word *ghayr* (other than) may be read in the nominative (raf'), the accusative (nasb), or the genitive (khafd).

The nominative has two possible readings. The first is that it means: "Is there any creator except God?" This has the sense of "there is no creator except God." The second is that it is a qualifier (na't) agreeing with the position of the noun (ʿalā al-mawḍiʿ), since the meaning is "Is there a creator other than God?" and *min* (from) is superfluous (zā'idah).

The accusative is in the sense of an exception (istithnā').

The genitive agrees with the wording (ʿalā al-lafẓ). Ḥumayd al-Ṭawīl said: I said to al-Ḥasan, "Who created evil?" He said, "Glory be to God! ﴿Is there any creator other than God?﴾ He created good and evil."

Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read *ghayru* in the genitive (*ghayri*). The rest read it in the nominative.

*Min al-ifk* (from the perversion): i.e., the rain. i.e., the plants.

*Min al-ifk* with a fatḥah (*al-afk*) means *al-ṣarf* (turning away). It is said: *mā afakaka ʿan kadhā*, meaning "what turned you away from such-and-such." It is also said: *min al-ifk* with a kasrah (*al-ifk*), which means lying. This too returns to the previous sense, because it is a statement turned away from truth and rightness. That is, from where does your denial of God's unity come to you?

The verse is a proof against the Qadariyya (those who deny divine predestination), because it negates any creator other than God, whereas they affirm creators alongside Him, as has been mentioned in more than one place.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 35, verse 4:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if they deny you﴾. That means the disbelievers of Quraysh. He consoles His Prophet and comforts him (ﷺ), and so that he may take as an example those before him in patience.

Al-Hasan, al-A'raj, Ya'qub, Ibn 'Amir, Abu Haywa, Ibn Muhaysin, Humayd, al-A'mash, Hamzah, Yahya, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read "turja'u" (with the tā' vowelled with a fatḥah), on the basis that it is the active form (musammā al-fā'il). Abu 'Ubayd preferred this reading, because of the saying of God, exalted is He: ﴿Surely to God all affairs are returned﴾ [al-Shura: 53]. The rest read "turja'u" (tuṛjaʿu, with the tā' vowelled with a ḍammah) as a passive verb (al-fi'l al-majhūl).

**The Qur'an, verse 5 of Surah 35:** "O mankind, indeed the promise of Allah is true, so let not the worldly life deceive you, and let not the Deceiver (al-gharur) deceive you concerning Allah."

Allah's statement: ﴿O mankind, indeed the promise of Allah is true﴾. This is an admonition to those who denied the Messenger, after the evidence for the truth of his statement had been made clear: that the Resurrection, the reward, and the punishment are true. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "The deception of the worldly life is that a person becomes preoccupied with its pleasures and delights to the neglect of the work of the Hereafter, until he says, 'Would that I had sent forth (good) for my life' (Qur'an 89:24)." Ibn al-Sikkit and Abu Hatim said: "al-gharur" is Satan. The word "gharur" is the plural of "gharr," and "gharr" is a verbal noun (masdar). "Al-gharur" may also be a verbal noun, but this is considered weak by others than Abu Ishaq, because "gharartuhu" is transitive, and the verbal noun of a transitive verb is generally of the pattern "fa'l" (as in "darabtuhu darban," "I struck him a blow"), except in a few small matters that cannot be used as a basis for analogy. They said: "lazimtuhu luzuman" (I stuck to him steadfastly) and "nahakahu al-marad nuhukan" (the illness wore him down). As for the meaning of the phrase, the best thing said about it is what Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "The deception concerning Allah is that a person commits sins and then wishes for forgiveness from Allah."

The reading of the majority is "al-gharur" (with a fatha on the ghayn), meaning Satan, i.e., let him not deceive you with his whisperings that he will overlook your sins because of your merit. Abu Haywa, Abu al-Mal al-Adawi and Muhammad ibn al-Muqa' read "al-ghurur" (with a damma on the ghayn), meaning falsehood, i.e., let not falsehood deceive you. Ibn al-Sikkit said: "al-ghurur" (with a damma) is what one is deceived by of the goods of the worldly life. Al-Zajjaj said: "It is also permissible that al-ghurur be the plural of 'ghar,' like 'qa'id' and 'qu'ud'." Al-Nahhas said: "Or the plural of 'gharr,' or it is likened to their saying 'nahakahu al-marad nuhukan' and 'lazimahu luzuman'." Al-Zamakhshari said: "Or the verbal noun of 'gharrahu,' like 'al-luzum' and 'al-nuhuk'."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 35, verse 6–7:

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, Satan is an enemy to you, so take him as an enemy﴾, meaning: be hostile to him and do not obey him. What points you to his enemy-hood is his expulsion of your father (Adam) from the Garden, and his guarantee to mislead you in the saying: ﴿And I will surely mislead them, and I will surely arouse in them desires﴾ [an-Nisa: 119], and the rest of the verse. And His saying: ﴿I will surely sit in wait for them on Your straight path. Then I will surely come to them from before them﴾ [al-A'raf: 16–17], and the rest of the verse. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has informed us that Satan is a clear enemy to us, and related to us his story and what he did to our father Adam (ﷺ), and how he undertook to be hostile to us and to deceive us, before our existence and after it. Yet we befriend him and obey him in what he wants from us, which is our ruin.

Al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyad used to say: "O liar, O deceiver! Fear Allah, and do not curse Satan in public while you are his friend in private."

Ibn as-Simmak said: "How strange is the one who disobeys the Benefactor after knowing His kindness, and obeys the accursed one after knowing his enmity!" This meaning has already been discussed in detail in al-Baqarah.

The word ''aduww (enemy) in His saying: ﴿Indeed, Satan is an enemy to you﴾ may be in the sense of mu'adin (one who is hostile), in which case it may be made dual, plural, or feminine. It may also be in the sense of a nisba (relative adjective), in which case it remains singular in every case, as Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿For indeed they are an enemy to me﴾ [ash-Shu'ara: 77]. According to this, the feminine is also 'aduww.

An-Nahhas said: As for the statement of some grammarians that the waw is "hidden" so they bring in the ha' (in the feminine form), it is an error; rather, the waw is a firm letter (ḥarf jald).

﴿Indeed he only invites his party﴾: "ma" (مَا) has prevented "inna" (إِنَّ) from governing, so a verb follows it. "Hizbahu" means his followers.

﴿That they may be among the companions of the Blaze﴾: this is his enmity. ﴿Those who disbelieve will have a severe punishment﴾. "Alladhina" may be a substitute (badal) for "ashab", so it is in the genitive position; or it may be a substitute for "hizbahu", so it is in the accusative position; or it may be a substitute for the waw (of the verb), so it is in the nominative position. A fourth view, and it is the best of them, is that it is in the nominative position as a subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is ﴿for them is a severe punishment﴾. It is as if He, glorified is He, has explained the condition of those who agree with Him and those who oppose Him, and the speech is complete at His saying: "from the companions of the Blaze." Then He begins, saying: ﴿Those who disbelieve, for them is a severe punishment﴾, also in the nominative position as a subject, and its predicate is (for them is forgiveness), meaning for their sins.

﴿And a great reward﴾, which is Paradise.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 35, verse 8:

His saying, Exalted is He: (Is then one to whom the evil of his deed is made attractive, so that he sees it as good...) "Man" (مَنْ) is in the nominative position as the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is omitted. Al-Kisa'i said: What indicates it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So let not your soul go out in regret over them﴾. The meaning is: Is then one to whom the evil of his deed is made attractive, so that he sees it as good [is like one who is guided]? Your soul would go out in regret over them. He said: This is a subtle Arabic expression that only a few understand. Al-Zamakhshari mentioned it from al-Zajjaj.

Al-Nahhas said: What al-Kisa'i said is the best of what has been said about the verse, because of what it indicates of the omitted element. The meaning is that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, forbade His Prophet from excessive distress over them and grief for them, as He said, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief﴾ [al-Kahf: 6]. The people of tafsir said: "Kill." 

Nasr ibn Ali said: I asked al-Asma'i about the saying of the Prophet ﷺ concerning the people of Yemen: "They are softer of heart and more abjectly obedient" (abkha'a ta'atan). What is the meaning of abkha'? He said: "Most sincere" (ansah). I said to him: The people of tafsir, Mujahid and others, say regarding Allah's saying, Mighty and Majestic, "Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief": its meaning is "killing yourself." He said: It is from that very same root; as if, from the intensity of his sincere advice to them, he was killing himself.

Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: There is inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in it. Its meaning: Is then one to whom the evil of his deed is made attractive, so that he sees it as good, [then] let not your soul go out in regret over them, for Allah leads astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills.

It was also said: the answer is omitted. The meaning: Is then one to whom the evil of his deed is made attractive equal to one who is guided? What indicates this omitted element is "For Allah leads astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills."

Yazid ibn al-Qa'qa' read: "So let not your soul go out..." (fa-la tadhhab nafsuka).

Regarding "Is then one to whom the evil of his deed is made attractive" there are four opinions. The first: they are the Jews, the Christians and the Magians; this is the view of Abu Qilaba. "The evil of his deed" would then be opposition to the Messenger, upon him be prayers and peace. The second: they are the Kharijites; this was narrated by Umar ibn al-Qasim. "The evil of his deed" would be the distortion of interpretation (tahrif al-ta'wil). The third: it is Satan; this is the view of al-Hasan. "The evil of his deed" would be misleading (al-ighwa'). The fourth: they are the disbelievers of Quraysh; this was said by al-Kalbi. "The evil of his deed" would be polytheism (al-shirk). He said: It was revealed concerning al-As ibn Wa'il al-Sahmi and al-Aswad ibn al-Muttalib. Others said: it was revealed concerning Abu Jahl ibn Hisham.

"And he sees it as good" means: correct (sawaban), said al-Kalbi. He also said: beautiful (jamilan).

I say: The view that the intended people are the disbelievers of Quraysh is the most evident of the opinions, because of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿It is not upon you to guide them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 272], and His saying: ﴿And let not those who hasten into disbelief grieve you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 176], and He said: ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself over their traces, if they do not believe in this narration, out of grief﴾ [al-Kahf: 6], and His saying: "Perhaps you would kill yourself that they will not be believers", and His saying in this verse. This is clear and manifest: that your grief over their persistence in disbelief will not benefit them, for Allah has misled them. This verse also refutes the Qadariyya in their saying mentioned earlier, namely: "Is then one to whom the evil of his deed is made attractive, so that he sees it as good" – you wish to guide him, but that is up to Allah, not to you; what is up to you is only conveying the message.

Abu Ja'far, Shayba and Ibn Muhaysin read: "Fa-la tudhhib" with a dammah on the ta' and a kasrah on the ha', "nafsuka" in the accusative as the object. The two meanings are close.

"Hasarat" is in the accusative as an object of cause (maf'ul min ajlihi), meaning: "So let not your soul go out for the regrets." "Alayhim" is the complement (silah) of "tadhhab", as you say: "He perished for love of him" (halaka 'alayhi hubban) and "he died of grief for him" (mata 'alayhi huznan). It clarifies the object of regret. It is not permissible for it to be connected to "hasarat", because the verbal noun (masdar) cannot have its complement placed before it. It is also permissible for it to be a circumstantial clause (hal), as if all of it had become regrets because of the intensity of the sorrow, as Jarir said:

Mashaqa al-hawajir lahmahunna ma'a al-sura ... wa-hatta dhahabna kalakilan wa-sudura

He means: they returned as only breasts and chests, i.e., nothing remained but their breasts and chests. And from this is the saying of another:

Fa-'ala ithrihim tasaqqatu nafsi ... wa-hasaratun wa-dhikruhum li siqam

Or it may be a verbal noun (masdar).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And it is Allah who sends the winds, and they stir up clouds, and We drive them to a dead land﴾. *Mayyit* and *mayt* are one and the same, and likewise *mayyita* and *mayta*. This is the view of the skilled (*al-ḥudhdhāq*) grammarians (*al-naḥwiyyūn*). Muhammad ibn Yazid said: "This is the view of the Basran grammarians (*al-baṣriyyūn*), and he excepted no one. He supported this with conclusive proofs." He recited:

*It is not the one who has died and found rest who is the dead one,*
*Rather, the dead one is the dead among the living.*

*The true dead is one who lives in misery,*
*With a downcast mind and little hope.*

He said: "Do you see any difference between *mayyit* and *mayt*?" He also recited:

*Hayyinūn, layyinūn, aysār banū yusr,*
*wa sawwās makrumatin abnā' aysār.*

He said: "They have agreed that *hayyinūn* and *layyinūn* are one, and likewise *mayyit* and *mayt*, and *sayyid* and *sayd*."

He said: "*Fa-saqnāhu* (we drove it) comes after saying *Wa-llāhu alladhī arsala al-riyāḥ* (And it is Allah who sends the winds), and this is from the shift of address (*talwīn al-khiṭāb*)." Abu Ubayda said: "Its proper form would be *fa-tasūquhu* (and it drives it), because He said *fa-tuthīru saḥāban* (and they stir up clouds)."

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask, why did *fa-tuthīru* come in the present tense (*al-muḍāraʿa*), unlike what precedes and follows it? I say: to depict the situation in which the stirring up of clouds by the winds takes place, and to bring before the mind that wondrous scene which indicates divine power. They do this with a verb that carries some distinction and particularity, for a situation that is strange, or that concerns the addressee, or for other reasons, as Ta'abbaṭa Sharran said:

*That I have met the ghūl (ogre) while it was swooping down,*
*and in a desert plain as smooth as a page;*
*So I struck it without fear, and it fell,*
*prostrate, upon its hands and its sides.*

He intended to portray for his people the situation in which, by his own claim, he bravely struck the ghūl, as if he were making them see it and informing them of its reality, to amaze them at his boldness in face of every terror and his steadfastness in every hardship." Likewise, since driving the clouds to a dead land is among the signs of overwhelming power, it was said *fa-saqnā* (We drove) and *aḥyaynā* (We gave life), shifted from the third-person form to what is more emphatic in particularity and more indicative of it."

The reading of the common people is *al-riyāḥ* (plural). Ibn Muḥayṣin, Ibn Kathir, al-A'mash, Yahya, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *al-rīḥ* (singular). The explanation of this verse and the discussion of it have already been given in full.

That is, thus you will be revived after you have died, from the raising of a human being to life (*nushūr*). So the *kāf* (the "thus") is in the position of nominative, meaning: like the giving of life to the dead is the raising of the dead.

On the authority of Abu Razin al-'Uqayli, who said: I said, "O Messenger of Allah, how does Allah revive the dead, and what is the sign of that in His creation?" He (ﷺ) said: "Did you not pass by the valley of your family barren and dry, then pass by it again greening and quivering?" I said, "Yes, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "So Allah revives the dead, and that is His sign in His creation."

We have mentioned this report in *al-A'rāf* and elsewhere.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 35, verse 10:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Whoever desires honour—then to Allah belongs all honour﴾. The estimated meaning according to al-Farra': "Whoever desires the knowledge (ʿilm) of honour." Others among the people of knowledge said likewise, meaning: whoever desires the knowledge of the honour that has no humiliation with it, because honour, if it leads to humiliation, is then only an exposure to humiliation; and the honour that has no humiliation in it belongs to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. "Jamiʿan" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥal). Al-Zajjaj estimated its meaning: whoever desires through his worship of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, honour—and honour belongs to Him, glorified be He—then Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, will honour him in the Hereafter and in this world. I say: this is the best, and it has been transmitted as a marfuʿ (raised) report, as will come. ﴿Then to Allah belongs all honour﴾: the apparent sense of this is to despair the listeners of His honour and to inform them that what is due to Him of that has no hope for anyone else; so the alif and lam are for the known reference (ʿahd) among those who know Him, glorified be He, and what is due to Him of that, and this is what is understood from His saying, the Truth, in Surah Yunus: ﴿And let not their saying grieve you; indeed, honour belongs to Allah﴾ [Yunus: 65]. It is also possible that He, glorified be He, intends to alert those of high rank and aspirations as to from where honour is attained and from where it is deserved, so the alif and lam are for totality (istighraq), and this is what is understood from the verses of this surah. Whoever seeks honour from Allah and is sincere in seeking it, with dependence, humility, stillness and submission, will find it with Him, if Allah wills, not withheld nor hidden from him. He ﷺ said: (Whoever humbles himself for Allah, Allah raises him). Whoever seeks it from other than Him, He leaves him to the one from whom he sought it. He has mentioned a people who sought honour from other than Him, saying: ﴿Those who take the disbelievers as allies instead of the believers—do they seek honour with them? Indeed, honour belongs entirely to Allah﴾ [An-Nisa: 139]. Thus He has informed you plainly, without any ambiguity, that honour belongs to Him; He honours by it whom He wills and humbles whom He wills. He ﷺ said, explaining His saying "Whoever desires honour—then to Allah belongs all honour": (Whoever desires the honour of both abodes, let him obey the Mighty). This is the meaning of al-Zajjaj's statement. Well did the one who said:

"When the necks humble themselves in humility and submission to You, their honour lies in their humbleness."

So whoever desires honour in order to attain the greatest success, and to enter the abode of honour—and to Allah belongs honour—let him aim with his honour at Allah, glorified be He, and the seeking of honour through Him; for whoever takes honour through a servant, Allah humbles him, and whoever takes honour through Allah, Allah honours him.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿To Him ascends the good word, and righteous deed raises it﴾. In it are two issues.

The first: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿To Him ascends the good word﴾, and the sentence is complete. Then you begin "and righteous deed raises it" in the sense: Allah raises it, or it raises its doer. It is also permissible that the meaning be: righteous deed raises the good word, so the sentence is connected, as its explanation will come. Ascent (ṣuʿūd) is movement upward, and it is also ʿurūj. This is not conceivable for speech, since it is an accident (ʿaraḍ), but its ascent is set forth as a parable for its acceptance, because the place of reward is above and the place of punishment is below. Al-Zajjaj said: it is said "the matter was raised to the judge," meaning he knew it, so it is in the sense of knowledge. Speech and deed are singled out for mention to clarify the reward for them. His saying "ilayhi" means: to Allah it ascends. It was said: it ascends to His heaven, and the place where no ruling applies to anyone other than Him. It was said: the book in which the servant's acts of obedience are written is carried up to heaven. The "good word" is tawhid proceeding from a good belief. It was said: it is praise and glorification, and the remembrance of Allah and the like. They recited:

"Do not be satisfied with a man's sweet speech until his action adorns what he says."

"When you weigh his action against his speech, and they balance, that brotherhood is beauty."

Ibn al-Muqaffaʿ said: speech without action is like a broth without fat, a cloud without rain, and a bow without a string. And concerning this it was said:

"Speech cannot be except with action, and every speech without action is vanity."

"Indeed, speech without action is beautiful, and marriage without a guardian is the same."

Al-Dahhak read "yuṣʿidu" with a damma on the yaʾ. The majority of people read "al-kalim", the plural of kalima. Abu ʿAbd al-Rahman read "al-kalam". I say: thus "al-kalam" may be used in the sense of "al-kalim" and vice versa, and on this is explained the saying of Abu al-Qasim: "The divisions of speech are three," where he placed "kalam" in the position of "kalim". And Allah knows best. "And righteous deed raises it": Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid and others said: the meaning is that righteous deed raises the good word. In a hadith: (Allah accepts no speech except with action, and accepts no speech and action except with intention, and accepts no speech, action and intention except with conformity to the Sunnah). Ibn ʿAbbas said: when the servant remembers Allah and speaks a good word and performs his obligations, his speech is raised along with his deed; and if he speaks without deed, his speech is returned to him. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: this is a view rejected by the belief of the people of the Sunnah, and it is not authentically reported from Ibn ʿAbbas. The truth is that the disobedient one who abandons the obligations, if he remembers Allah and speaks a good word, then it is recorded for him and accepted from him, and he has his good deeds and against him his bad deeds; and Allah, the Exalted, accepts from everyone who guards against shirk. Also, the good word is itself a righteous deed, and the statement of one who says that deed is what raises speech is only sound if it is interpreted as meaning that it increases its elevation and its good standing when it accompanies it—just as the one who has deeds of prayer, fasting and other acts, when a good word and the remembrance of Allah intersperse his deeds, the deeds become more noble. So the saying "and righteous deed raises it" becomes an admonition, a reminder and an exhortation to deeds. As for statements which are themselves deeds, such as tawhid and tasbih, they are accepted. Ibn al-ʿArabi said: "The speech of a person in the remembrance of Allah, if it is not joined with righteous deed, does not benefit, because whoever's speech contradicts his action, it is a burden upon him. The verification of this is: that when deed becomes a condition for the acceptance of speech or is bound to it, then there is no acceptance for it without it; and if it is not a condition for it, then his good word is written for him and his evil deed is written against him, and a weighing takes place between them, then Allah decides success, profit or loss." I say: what Ibn al-ʿArabi said is not a verification. The apparent meaning is that righteous deed is a condition for the acceptance of the good word. It has come in reports: "When the servant says, 'There is no god but Allah,' with a sincere intention, the angels look at his deed; if the deed conforms to his saying, both ascend together; and if his deed contradicts it, his saying is halted until he repents of his deed." Based on this, righteous deed raises the good word to Allah. The pronoun in "yarfaʿuhu" returns to the good word. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas, Shahr ibn Hawshab, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, Qatada, Abu al-ʿAliya and al-Dahhak. And on the view that "the good word" is tawhid, it is what raises righteous deed, because righteous deed is not accepted except with faith and tawhid; i.e., "and righteous deed raises it" means the good word raises the righteous deed, so the pronoun returns to the righteous deed. This view was also reported from Shahr ibn Hawshab, who said: "The good word" is the Qur'an, "and righteous deed raises it" is the Qur'an. It was also said: the pronoun returns to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, meaning that righteous deed is raised by Allah above the good word, because deed is the realization of speech, and the doer is more toiling than the speaker; and this is the literal sense of the statement, because Allah is the Raiser and the Abaser. The second and the first are figurative, but it is permissible. Al-Nahhas said: the first view is the most preferable and soundest, because of the high rank of those who held it, and because in Arabic it is preferable, since the readers read "deed" in the nominative. Had the meaning been "and righteous deed raises it, Allah," or "righteous deed is raised by the good word," the preference would have been half the deed. We know of no one who read it in the accusative except something reported from ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar, that he said: some people read "wal-ʿamala al-ṣāliḥa yarfaʿuhu Allah" (the accusative "al-ʿamal"). It was also said: righteous deed raises its doer, and this is the one who desired honour and knew that it is sought from Allah, the Exalted; mentioned by al-Qushayri.

The second issue: They mentioned in the presence of Ibn ʿAbbas that a dog cuts off prayer, so he recited this verse: "To Him ascends the good word, and righteous deed raises it." This is an argument by generality according to the position of the early scholars on the principle of generality, (and whoever enters prayer with its conditions, nothing cuts it off for him except by establishing what requires that, from the like of what the prayer was established by, from the Qur'an, Sunnah or consensus). Whoever held that view relied on his saying, peace be upon him: (A woman, a donkey and a black dog cut off prayer). I said: what about the black dog as opposed to the white dog and the red dog? He said: (The black one is a devil). Muslim transmitted it. There is also what opposes this, which al-Bukhari transmitted from the nephew of Ibn Shihab, that he asked his uncle about whether anything cuts off prayer; he said: nothing cuts it off. ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr informed me that ʿAisha, wife of the Prophet ﷺ, said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to stand and pray at night, and I was lying across between him and the qibla on his family's bedding.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those who plot evil deeds—for them is severe punishment, and the plotting of those will perish﴾. Al-Tabari mentioned in (Kitab Adab al-Nufus): Yunus ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿla told me, saying: Sufyan told us, from Layth ibn Abi Sulaym, from Shahr ibn Hawshab al-Ashʿari, concerning His saying, mighty and majestic: "And those who plot evil deeds—for them is severe punishment, and the plotting of those will perish," he said: they are the people of showing off (riyaʾ); this is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid and Qatada. Abu al-ʿAliya said: they are those who plotted against the Prophet ﷺ when they gathered in the Dar al-Nadwa. Al-Kalbi said: meaning those who do evil deeds, "as-sayyiʾat" being in the world. Muqatil said: meaning shirk, so "as-sayyiʾat" would be the object. It is said: "bara yabūru" means it perished and became void, and "the market was bara" meaning it went slack; from this: "We seek refuge in Allah from the perishing of the unmarried woman" [the unmarried woman is one without a husband]. And His saying: "and you were a people perishing" [al-Fath: 12], meaning those who were destroyed. And "al-makr" is what is done by way of trickery and deception. It has already passed in Surah Saba' [see p. 302 of this volume].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 35, verse 11:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah created you from dust, then from a drop of semen﴾. Sa'id reported from Qatadah that he said: "It means Adam, peace be upon him, and the meaning according to this is: He created your origin (asl) from dust." He said: "That is, the one He brought forth from your fathers' loins." He said: "That is, He paired some of you with others, so the male is a mate (zawj) to the female, in order to complete the survival in this world until its term ends."

﴿And no female conceives or gives birth except with His knowledge﴾. That is, He made you into pairs, so the male marries the female and they produce offspring by the knowledge of Allah. Thus there is no pregnancy or delivery except that Allah knows it, and nothing departs from His management.

﴿Nor is one given a long life (yu'ammar), nor is any of his life shortened, except that it is in a Book﴾. He called him "one given a long life" (mu'ammar) because of what he is destined to become. Sa'id ibn Jubayr reported from Ibn Abbas: "'Nor is one given a long life' — no one who is given a long life has his lifespan recorded, how many years, how many months, how many days, how many hours; then it is written in another book: a day has been subtracted from his life, a month has been subtracted, a year has been subtracted, until he completes his term." Sa'id ibn Jubayr also said: "What has passed of his term is the shortening, and what is yet to come is what he is given a long life in, so the pronoun in this view refers to the one given a long life." And from Sa'id also: "His lifespan is recorded as so many years, then at the bottom of that is written: a day has passed, two days have passed, until it reaches its end."

From Qatadah: the one given a long life is the one who reaches sixty years, and the one whose life is shortened is the one who dies before sixty years.

Al-Farra' said regarding "Nor is one given a long life": what is meant is that none of his lifespan is added to, "nor is any of his life shortened" in another sense, that is, nor is the other person's life shortened except that it is in a Book. So the pronoun in "his life" refers to another, not the first, and he referred to it with the pronoun as if it were the first, like your saying: "I have a dirham and its half," meaning half of another.

It was also said: Allah recorded the lifespan of a human as one hundred years if he obeys, and ninety if he disobeys; whichever of the two he reaches, it is in the Book. This is like his saying, peace be upon him: "Whoever wishes that his provision be expanded for him and his term (in his trace) be prolonged for him, let him maintain his ties of kinship." That is, it is written in the Preserved Tablet: "So-and-so's lifespan is such-and-such years; if he maintains his ties of kinship, such-and-such years will be added to his life." Then it is clarified in another place of the Preserved Tablet that he will maintain his ties of kinship. Whoever looks at the first and not the second thinks there is an addition or a reduction. This meaning has already been discussed at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah erases what He wills and confirms﴾ [al-Ra'd: 39], and the pronoun on this view refers to the lifespan.

It was also said: the meaning is "Nor is one given a long life" — that is, one who has become decrepit (harim) — "and no other's lifespan of the decrepit is shortened except that it is in a Book," that is, by the decree of Allah, mighty and majestic. This meaning was narrated from al-Dahhak, and al-Nahhas chose it, saying: "It is the most similar of these to the apparent sense of the revelation." A similar view was narrated from Ibn Abbas. The pronoun on this view may refer to the one given a long life, and it may refer to someone other than the one given a long life, meaning that the recording of deeds and terms is not impossible for Him.

The recitation of the common readers is "yunqasu" with a dammah on the yaa' and a fathah on the qaaf. A group among them, including Ya'qub, read "yanqusu" with a fathah on the yaa' and a dammah on the qaaf, meaning: nothing is diminished from his lifespan. It is said: naqasa al-shay' by itself and naqasahu others, and zada by itself and zadahu others, transitive and intransitive. Al-A'raj and al-Zuhri read "min 'umurihi" with the mim lightened, while the rest read it with a dammah on the mim; they are two dialects, like al-suhq and al-suhuq. And "yasir" means: counting the long-lived and the short-lived is not difficult for Him; none of them is inaccessible to Him or escapes Him. As for its grammar: "yasir" (easy) is of the pattern fa'il, and if you named a person by it, it would be diptote (ghayr munsarif), because it is of the pattern fa'il.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 35, verse 12:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the two seas are not alike: this one is sweet, pleasant to drink, and this one is salty, bitter.﴾ On this there are four issues.

The first issue: Ibn 'Abbas said: "Furat" is sweet, and "ujaj" is bitter. Talhah recited "hadha milhun ujajun" with a fatha on the mim and a kasra on the lam, without an alif. As for the "salty" (mali'h), it is that in which salt is put. 'Isa and Ibn Abi Ishaq recited "sayyigh sharabuhu" (سَيِّغٌ شَرَابُهُ), on the pattern of sayyid and mayyit. There is no disagreement that it comes from both of them together. The discussion of this has already passed in "al-Nahl."

The second issue: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and from both you extract ornaments which you wear﴾. The view of Abu Ishaq (al-Zajjaj) is that the ornament is only extracted from the salt water, and it was said "from both" because they are mixed. Others said: what is extracted are the shells in which the ornament is, namely pearls and other things, from the places where there is sweet and salt water, such as the springs; so it is taken from both, because in the sea there are sweet springs, and between them pearls come forth at the point of mixing. It was also said: from the rain of the sky. Muhammad ibn Yazid (al-Mubarrad) gave a fourth view, saying: the ornament is extracted only from the salt water. Al-Nahhas said: this is the best of these views, and it is not what he meant, because they are mixed; rather it is a grouping in which he informs about one of them, as He, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿And out of His mercy He made for you the night and the day, that you may rest therein and that you may seek of His bounty﴾ [al-Qasas: 73]. And as you say: "If you saw al-Hasan and al-Hajjaj, you would see good and evil." And as you say: "If you saw al-A'mash and Sibawayh, you would fill your hand with lexicon and grammar." The meaning of this is known, and it is abundant eloquent speech. Thus: ﴿and from each you eat fresh flesh and extract ornaments which you wear﴾; so the two agree in the first and the salt is singled out for the second.

The third issue: In His saying "which you wear" there is evidence that the wearing of each thing is according to its kind: the ring is placed on the finger, the bracelet on the forearm, the necklace on the neck, and the anklet on the leg. In al-Bukhari and al-Nasa'i, from Ibn Sirin, who said: I said to 'Abidah: is spreading silk the same as wearing it? He said: Yes. And in the Sahih, from Anas: "I stood on a mat of ours which had become black from much use." The hadith.

The fourth issue: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and you see the ships ploughing through it﴾. Al-Nahhas said: that is, the water of the salt sea specifically; had it not been so, He would have said "in them both." The ship "makhara" (تَمْخُرُ) when it cleaves the water. This has already passed in "al-Nahl." Mujahid said: it is trade by ships to distant lands in a short period, as has passed in "al-Baqarah." It was also said: what is extracted from its ornament and what is hunted from its fish.

﴿And that you may be grateful﴾ for what He has given you of His bounty. It was said: for what He has saved you from its terror.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 35, verse 13:

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿He causes the night to enter into the day and causes the day to enter into the night﴾. This has already been discussed in (Surat Al 'Imran) and elsewhere.

(And He has subjected the sun and the moon, each running for a specified term.) Its explanation has already been given in (Surat Luqman).

(That is Allah, your Lord; to Him belongs dominion.) That is: this One, whose handiwork is this, is the established Creator and Manager, the Capable and Powerful. So He alone is to be worshipped. He means the idols. (...) ﴿qitmir﴾, that is, they have no power over it, nor over creating it. Al-Qitmir is the thin white membrane that lies between the date and the pit, so said most of the exegetes. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is the split of the pit (nawat), and this is the view chosen by al-Mubarrad, and Qatadah said likewise. It is also reported from Qatadah: al-Qitmir is the cap that is on the top of the pit. Al-Jawhari said: it is said that it is the white speck that is on the back of the pit, from which the palm tree grows.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 35, verse 14:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿If you call upon them, they will not hear your call﴾. That is, if you seek help from them in calamities, they will not hear your call, because they are inanimate objects that neither see nor hear, since not everything that hears is able to speak. Qatadah said: the meaning is that even if they heard, they would not benefit you. It was also said: that is, if We had given them intellect and life so that they heard your call, they would have been more obedient to God than you are, and they would not have responded to you in disbelief.

﴿And on the Day of Resurrection they will deny your association﴾, that is, they will deny that you worshipped them, and will disown you. It is also permissible that this refers to those worshipped who have intellect, such as the angels, the jinn, the prophets and the devils, meaning that they will deny that what you did was true and that they had commanded you to worship them, as He reported about Jesus in His saying: "It is not for me to say what I have no right to say" [[See vol. 6, p. 374]] [al-Ma'idah: 116]. It is also permissible that idols are included in this, meaning that God will give them life until they declare that they were not worthy of worship.

[He is God, may He be mighty and majestic]. That is, no one is better informed about the creation of God than God Himself, so none can inform you like Him about His affairs. [[In manuscripts B and H: "upon him."]]

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 35, verse 15:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O mankind, you are the poor toward Allah﴾, i.e., those who are in need of Him for your existence and in all your circumstances. Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask, why did He define 'the poor' (with the definite article)? I say: He intended by this to show them that, because of the intensity of their need for Him, they are the very class of the poor, even though all creatures, among humankind and others, are in need of Him, because poverty follows weakness, and the poorer the one in need, the weaker he is. Allah, glorified is He, has testified concerning man to his weakness in His saying: ﴿And man was created weak﴾ [[see vol. 5, p. (168)]]

[al-Nisa': 28], and He said: ﴿Allah is the One who created you from weakness﴾ [[see vol. 46 of this part.]]

[al-Rum: 54]. Had He used the indefinite, the meaning would be: 'You are some of the poor.' If you ask: 'The poor' has been contrasted with 'the Rich (al-Ghaniyy)', so what is the benefit of 'the Praiseworthy (al-Hamid)'? I say: When He established their poverty toward Him and His independence from them, and not every rich person is beneficial by his wealth unless the wealthy one is generous and bountiful, and when he is generous and bestows favours, those upon whom he bestows favours praise him and he deserves praise from them, He mentioned 'the Praiseworthy' to indicate that He is the Rich who benefits His creation by His wealth, the Generous who bestows favours upon them, the One deserving, by His bestowing favours upon them, that they praise Him." The softening of the second hamza is, according to al-Khalil, the best of the forms, and it is permissible to soften the first alone, to soften both, or to realize both fully. As for "And Allah is the Rich, the Praiseworthy," the "huwa" may be superfluous (za'ida), so it has no place in i'rab, or it may be a beginning (mubtada'), in which case its place is nominative (raf').

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 35, verse 16–17:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿If He wills, He will remove you﴾. There is an elision in it; the meaning is "If He wills [that [[addition from al-Nahhas.]]] He remove you" — "He will remove you," that is, He will annihilate you.

(And bring a new creation) — that is, more obedient than you and purer.

(And that is not difficult for Allah) — that is, not unattainable, not hard, not impossible. This has already been discussed in (Ibrahim) [[see vol. 9, p. 354]].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 35, verse 16–17:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿If He wills, He will remove you﴾. There is an elision in it; the meaning is "If He wills [that [[addition from al-Nahhas.]]] He remove you" — "He will remove you," that is, He will annihilate you.

(And bring a new creation) — that is, more obedient than you and purer.

(And that is not difficult for Allah) — that is, not unattainable, not hard, not impossible. This has already been discussed in (Ibrahim) [[see vol. 9, p. 354]].

The discussion of this has already been covered (see vol. 7, p. 157), and it is disconnected from what precedes it. The original form is "tu'zar" (تؤزر), in which the wāw was dropped to match "yazir" (يَزِرُ). "Wāziratun" (وازِرَةٌ) is a qualifier of an omitted noun, meaning "nafsun wāziratun" (a soul bearing a burden). Likewise, in "wa-in tadu muthqalatun ila ḥimlihā" (وَإِنْ تَدْعُ مُثْقَلَةٌ إِلى حِمْلِها), al-Farra' said: that is, "nafsun muthqalatun" (a burdened soul) or "dābbatun" (a beast). He said: this applies to both the masculine and the feminine.

Al-Akhfash said: that is, "wa-in tadu muthqalatun insānan ilā ḥimlihā," and that burden is her sins. The "ḥiml" (الحِمْل) is what is carried on the back, while "ḥaml" (الحَمْل) is the pregnancy of a woman and the fruit of a date palm; al-Kisa'i related both with a fatḥa only, and no other vowelling. Ibn al-Sikkit related that the "ḥaml" of the date palm may be pronounced with either fatḥa or kasra.

"Lā yuḥmalu minhu shay'un wa-law kāna dhā qurbā" (لَا يُحْمَلْ مِنْهُ شَيْءٌ وَلَوْ كانَ ذَا قُرْبى): according to al-Akhfash's view, the estimate is "wa-law kāna al-insānu al-madʿuwwu dhā qurbā" (even if the person called upon were a relative). Al-Farra' permitted "wa-law kāna dhū qurbā." This is permissible according to Sibawayh, and similar to it is "wa-in kāna dhū ʿusratin" (وَإِنْ كانَ ذُو عُسْرَةٍ) [al-Baqarah: 280], where "kāna" then carries the meaning of "waqaʿa" (occurred), or the predicate is omitted, meaning: "wa-in kāna fīmun tuṭālibūna dhū ʿusratin" (and if among those you demand from there is one in hardship). Sibawayh related: "al-nāsu majziyyūna bi-aʿmālihim, in khayrun fa-khayrun" (people are recompensed for their deeds: if good, then good), according to this view; and "khayran fa-khayrun" according to the first.

It is related from Ikrimah that he said: It has reached me that a Jew or a Christian sees a Muslim man on the Day of Resurrection and says to him: "Did I not do you a kindness? Did I not treat you well?" He says: "Yes." He says: "Then benefit me." The Muslim keeps asking Allah, the Exalted, until some of His punishment is lessened for him. And a man comes to his father on the Day of Resurrection and says: "Was I not dutiful to you, caring for you, and good to you, and you see what I am in? So grant me a good deed of yours, or bear a sin on my behalf." He says: "What you ask of me is small, but I fear what you fear." And a father says the same to his son, and he replies with something similar. And a man says to his wife: "Did I not treat you well in marriage? So bear a sin for me, that perhaps I may be saved." She says: "That is indeed small, but I fear what you fear." Then Ikrimah recited: "Wa-in tadu muthqalatun ila ḥimlihā lā yuḥmalu minhu shay'un wa-law kāna dhā qurbā."

Al-Fuḍayl ibn ʿIyāḍ said: it is the woman who meets her child and says: "O my child, did not my belly hold you as a vessel? Did not my breast give you drink? Did not my lap cradle you?" He says: "Yes, O mother." She says: "O my son, my sins have burdened me, so bear one sin of mine for me." He says: "Away from me, O mother, for I am occupied with my own sin."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿إِنَّما تُنْذِرُ الَّذِينَ يَخْشَوْنَ رَبَّهُمْ بِالْغَيْبِ﴾ means: only those who fear the punishment of Allah, the Exalted, accept your warning. It is like His saying, exalted is He: "innamā tundhiru man ittabaʿa al-dhikra wa-khashiya al-raḥmāna bi-al-ghayb" (You only warn those who follow the Reminder and fear the Most Merciful unseen) [Yā-Sīn: 11]. [See p. 9 of this part, after verse 11 of Surat Yā-Sīn.]

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿وَمَنْ تَزَكَّى فَإِنَّما يَتَزَكَّى لِنَفْسِهِ﴾ means: whoever is guided, is guided only for his own self. It was also read: "wa-man izzakkā fa-innamā yuzakkā li-nafsihi" (وَمَنِ ازَّكَّى فَإِنَّمَا يَزَّكَّى لِنَفْسِهِ).

(وَإِلَى اللَّهِ الْمَصِيرُ) means: to Him is the return of all creation.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 35, verse 19–22:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the blind and the seeing are not alike﴾, i.e., the disbeliever and the believer, the ignorant and the knowledgeable. Like His saying: "Say: The bad and the good are not equal" [al-Ma'idah: 100]. [[See vol. 6, p. 327.]]

(Nor are the darknesses and the light) Al-Akhfash Sa'id said: "la" is superfluous, and the meaning is: nor are the darknesses and the light, nor the shade and the scorching heat. Al-Akhfash said: al-harur (scorching heat) occurs only with the sunshine of the day, while al-samum (hot wind) occurs at night; and it was said the reverse. Ru'bah ibn al-Ajjaj said: al-harur occurs specifically by day and al-samum occurs specifically by night; related by al-Mahdawi. Al-Farra' said: al-samum occurs only by day, and al-harur occurs in both. Al-Nahhas said: this is more correct, because harur is on the pattern fa'ul from harr (heat), and it carries the sense of intensification, i.e., the harmful heat. I say: In Sahih Muslim, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "The Fire said: 'My Lord, some of me consumed others of me, so permit me to breathe.' So He permitted it two breaths: one breath in winter and one breath in summer. So whatever cold or freezing you find is from the breath of Jahannam, and whatever heat or scorching you find is from the breath of Jahannam." And it was narrated from the hadith of al-Zuhri, from Sa'id, from Abu Hurayrah: "What heat you find is from its samum, and the intensity of cold you find is from its zamharir." This gathers those sayings, and that samum and harur occur both by night and by day, so reflect on it. It was also said: what is meant by the shade and the harur is Paradise and Hellfire: Paradise has perpetual shade, as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Its fruit is everlasting and its shade﴾ [al-Ra'd: 35] [[See vol. 9, p. 324.]], and Hellfire has scorching heat. Al-Suddi said the same. Ibn 'Abbas said: i.e., the shade of the night and the heat of the samum by day. Qutrub said: al-harur is heat, and al-zill is cold.

(Nor are the living and the dead alike) Ibn Qutaybah said: the living are the intelligent, and the dead are the ignorant. Qatadah said: all of these are parables, i.e., just as these things are not equal, so too the disbeliever and the believer are not equal.

(Indeed Allah causes to hear whom He wills) i.e., He causes His friends to hear, those whom He created for His Paradise.

(And you cannot make those in the graves hear) i.e., the disbelievers whose hearts disbelief has caused to die; just as you cannot make the dead hear, so too you cannot make hear the one whose heart has died. Al-Hasan, 'Isa al-Thaqafi and 'Amr ibn Maymun read: "bi-musmi'in man fi al-qubur" with the tanwin dropped for lightness, meaning: they are in the position of the people of the graves in that they do not benefit from what they hear and do not accept it.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the blind and the seeing are not alike﴾, i.e., the disbeliever and the believer, the ignorant and the knowledgeable. Like His saying: "Say: The bad and the good are not equal" [al-Ma'idah: 100]. [[See vol. 6, p. 327.]]

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 35, verses 27–28:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Have you not seen that Allah sends down water from the sky﴾. This seeing is seeing of the heart and of knowledge, meaning: "Has your knowledge not reached [the point] that you see with your heart that Allah sent down...?" So "anna" (that) with its noun and predicate stands in place of the two objects of "ra'a" (to see). ﴿So We brought forth thereby fruits﴾: this is from the shift of address (talwin al-khitab). ﴿Varying in their colours﴾: "mukhtalifan" is in the accusative as an adjective (na't) of "thamarat" (fruits). "Alwanuha" (their colours) is in the nominative as the agent of "mukhtalif," and it is suitable for it to be an adjective of "thamarat" because of the pronoun that returns to it from its mention. In other than the Qur'an it is permissible to make it nominative, and similar to it is: "I saw a man whose father is going out" (khariljan abuhu). "Bihi" (by it) means by the water, which is one, while the fruits are varied.

(And of the mountains are streaks, white and red, varying in their colours.) "Judad" is the plural of "judda," which are the varied-coloured tracts, even if the whole is stone or earth. Al-Akhfash said: If it were the plural of "jadid" he would have said "judud" (with a kasra on the jim and a damma on the dal), like sarir and surur. Zuhayr said:

As if he were a dark-cheeked one with streaks, lean, and grazing naked after the summer.

It is also said that the "judad" are pieces (qita'), derived from "jaddadtu al-shay'" when I cut it; this was related by Ibn Bahr. Al-Jawhari said: "al-judda" is the mark on the back of a donkey that differs from its colour; "al-judda" is also a path, and the plural is "judad." Allah the Exalted said: "And of the mountains are streaks, white and red, varying in their colours," meaning tracts that differ from the colour of the mountain. From this comes their saying: "So-and-so rode a judda of the matter," when he took an opinion in it. And "kisa'un mujaddad" is a garment with varied lines. Al-Zamakhshari said: al-Zuhri read "judud" with a damma, the plural of "jadida," which is "al-jiddah." It is said: jadida, judud, and jadha'id, like safina, sufun, and safa'in. Abu Dhu'ayb's verse has been interpreted with this:

Dark of the back, it has four streaks...

[Its first half: "And time does not remain upon its vicissitudes..."]

It is also related from him as "jadad" with two fathas, which is the clear, manifest path, placed in the position of the clear, distinct tracts and lines, some separated from others.

(And of mankind and beasts) It is also read "wad-dawabbi" with a light (tashdid-less) ba. A parallel to this lightening is the reading of whoever read "wa la al-dallin" (and not the astray), because each of them fled from the meeting of two sukun, so the first was given a fatha and the last was dropped; this was said by al-Zamakhshari.

(And of the cattle, their colours vary.) That is, among them are red, white, black, and other colours, and all of that is evidence of a Creator who chooses. He said "mukhtalifun alwanuhu" and so made the pronoun masculine in agreement with "min" (some); this was said by al-Mu'arrij. Abu Bakr ibn Ayyash said: he mentioned the pronoun only because it refers to an implied "ma" (that which), the meaning being: "and of mankind, and of beasts, and of cattle, is that whose colours vary," that is, white, red, and black.

(And dark black.) Abu Ubayda said: "al-Ghirbib" is the intensely black; so in the sentence there is inversion, and the meaning is: "and of the mountains, black, intensely black." The Arabs say of the intensely black whose colour is like the colour of a crow: "aswad ghirbib." Al-Jawhari said: you say "hadha aswad ghirbib," meaning very black. When you say "gharabib sud," you make "sud" a substitute (badal) for "gharabib," because the emphasis of colours does not precede. In a hadith from the Prophet ﷺ: "Indeed Allah dislikes the old man who dyes himself black," meaning one who dyes with black. Imru' al-Qays said:

The eye is roving, the hand is swimming, and the leg is sweeping, and the face is ghirbib.

[This is the reading of the originals. The verse as it appears in his Diwan (Matba'at al-Istiqama) is:

The hand swimming, the leg thrusting, the eye piercing, the back smooth...]

Another said describing a vine:

And among the wonders of Allah's creation is a spreading vine, from which is pressed the white and the black (ghirbib) [wine].

(Thus) here is the completion of the speech, meaning: thus the states of the servants differ in fear. Then he resumed and said: ﴿Only those of His servants who have knowledge fear Allah. Indeed Allah is Mighty, Forgiving﴾. By "the scholars" are meant those who fear His power; whoever knows that He, Mighty and Majestic, is capable, is certain of His punishment for disobedience, as 'Ali ibn Abi Talha related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding "Only those of His servants who have knowledge fear Allah": he said, "Those who know that Allah is over all things capable." al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: whoever does not fear Allah the Exalted is not a scholar. Mujahid said: The scholar is only one who fears Allah, Mighty and Majestic. From Ibn Mas'ud: Fear of Allah the Exalted is sufficient as knowledge, and self-delusion is sufficient as ignorance. It was said to Sa'd ibn Ibrahim: "Who is the most learned of the people of Madina?" He said: "The most God-fearing of them toward their Lord, Mighty and Majestic." From Mujahid, he said: The jurist is only one who fears Allah, Mighty and Majestic. From 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, he said: The true jurist is one who does not make people despair of Allah's mercy, does not permit them to disobey Allah the Exalted, does not make them feel secure from Allah's punishment, and does not abandon the Qur'an in preference for something else. There is no good in worship without knowledge, nor knowledge without understanding, nor recitation without reflection. Al-Darimi Abu Muhammad transmitted from Makhul, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Indeed the virtue of the scholar over the worshipper is like my virtue over the least of you," then he recited this verse: "Only those of His servants who have knowledge fear Allah. Indeed Allah and His angels and the inhabitants of His heavens and the inhabitants of His earth, and even the ant in its hole and the fish in the sea, send blessings upon those who teach people good." The report is mursal. Al-Darimi said: Abu al-Nu'man related to me, from Hammad ibn Zayd, from Yazid ibn Hazim, who said: my paternal uncle Jarir ibn Zayd related to me [in the originals: "Jarir ibn Yazid," which is an error; see Tahdhib al-Tahdhib and Sunan al-Darimi] that he heard Tubay' narrate from Ka'b, who said: "I find the description of a people who learn for other than action, who gain understanding for other than worship, who seek the world by the deeds of the Hereafter, who wear sheepskins while their hearts are more bitter than aloes; by Me they are deceived, and at Me they scheme. By Myself I swear that I will send upon them a trial that leaves the forbearing among them bewildered." It was narrated by al-Tirmidhi as marfu' from the hadith of Abu al-Darda', and we have written it in the introduction of the book [see vol. 1, p. 19 onward].

Al-Zamakhshari: If you ask, what is the reading of whoever reads "innama yakhsha Allah" with a damma on the Name and "min 'ibadihi al-'ulama'" with a fatha on the last word, which is 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, and is attributed to Abu Hanifa? I say: "khashya" in this reading is a metaphor, and the meaning is: he honours and magnifies them, as a dreaded, awe-inspiring man is honoured among people, from among all His servants.

(Indeed Allah is Mighty, Forgiving.) This is a reason for the obligation of fear, since it indicates His punishment of the disobedient and His subjugation of them, and His reward of the people of obedience and His pardon of them. And the one who punishes and rewards is deserving of being feared.

There are four issues here. **The first:** this verse is problematic, because He, Mighty and Majestic, says ﴿Then We gave the Book to those whom We have chosen from among Our servants﴾ and then says ﴿Among them is one who wrongs himself﴾. Al-Nahhas said: Among the soundest of what has been reported on this is what is narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿Among them is one who wrongs himself﴾, that he said: "The disbeliever." It was related by Ibn Uyayna from Amr ibn Dinar from Ata from Ibn Abbas as well. And also from Ibn Abbas, regarding ﴿Among them is one who wrongs himself, and among them is one who is moderate, and among them is one who is foremost in good deeds﴾, he said: "Two groups are saved." In Arabic the construction would be: "Among them, from among Our servants, is one who wrongs himself," meaning a disbeliever. Al-Hasan said: meaning a sinner (fasiq). The pronoun in ﴿they will enter it﴾ refers to the moderate and the foremost, not to the wrongdoer. It was reported from Ikrimah, Qatadah, al-Dahhak and al-Farra' that the moderate is the believer who disobeys, and the foremost is the pious person without qualification. They said: This verse is similar to His saying, Exalted is He, in Surah al-Waqi'ah: ﴿And you will be three groups﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 7], and so on. They said: It is far-fetched that one who is chosen should be a wrongdoer. It was also narrated by Mujahid from Ibn Abbas. Mujahid said: ﴿Among them is one who wrongs himself﴾ refers to the companions of the left (ashab al-mash'amah), ﴿and among them is one who is moderate﴾ refers to the companions of the right (ashab al-maymanah), and ﴿among them is one who is foremost in good deeds﴾ refers to the foremost among all people. It was also said: the pronoun in ﴿they will enter it﴾ refers to all three categories, on the condition that the wrongdoer here is neither a disbeliever nor a sinner. Among those from whom this view is reported are Umar, Uthman, Abu'l-Darda', Ibn Mas'ud, Uqbah ibn Amr and A'ishah. The interpretation according to this view is that the wrongdoer to himself is one who committed minor sins. As for "the moderate," Muhammad ibn Yazid said: he is one who gives the world its due and the Hereafter its due. Thus ﴿Gardens of perpetual residence, they will enter them﴾ refers to all of them according to this explanation and clarification. It was reported from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri. Ka'b al-Ahbar said: "Their shoulders are level, by the Lord of the Ka'bah, and they differ by their deeds." Abu Ishaq al-Sabi'i said: "As for what I have heard for sixty years, all of them are saved." Usamah ibn Zayd narrated that the Prophet ﷺ recited this verse and said: "All of them are in Paradise." Umar ibn al-Khattab recited this verse and then said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Our foremost is foremost, our moderate is saved, and our wrongdoer is forgiven." According to this view, the object of the verb of choosing in His saying, ﴿We have given the Book to those whom We have chosen from among Our servants﴾, is considered to be an omitted genitive (mudaf) construction, as the omitted mudaf occurs in ﴿And ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82], meaning: We chose their religion. Then what remains is "We chose them," so the returning pronoun to the relative clause (al-'a'id ila'l-mawsul) is omitted, as it is omitted in His saying, ﴿And I do not say to those whom your eyes look down upon﴾ [Hud: 31], meaning: whom your eyes look down upon. Thus the choosing is directed to their religion, as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, Allah has chosen for you the religion﴾ [al-Baqarah: 132]. Al-Nahhas said: There is a third view: the wrongdoer is the one who commits major sins, and the moderate is the one who does not deserve Paradise by having his good deeds outweigh his bad deeds. Thus ﴿Gardens of perpetual residence, they will enter them﴾ applies only to those who were foremost in good deeds. This is the view of a group of people of reflection, because in the strict sense of reasoning the pronoun should refer to what is nearest to it. I say: The middle view is the best and the most sound, if Allah wills, because the disbeliever and the hypocrite were not chosen, praise be to Allah, and their religion was not chosen. This is the view of six of the Companions, and that is sufficient for you. We shall elaborate and clarify it further in the rest of the verse.

Here "the Book" is meant to include the meanings of the Book, its knowledge, its rulings and its creed. It is as though Allah, when He gave the Qur'an to the Ummah of Muhammad ﷺ, and it included the meanings of the revealed Books, He thereby bequeathed to the Ummah of Muhammad, peace be upon him, the Book that was among the nations before us.

(Isṭafaynā) means We chose. Its derivation is from ṣafw, which is purity, freedom from the impurities of turbidity. Its original form is iṣtafawnā, then the tā' was changed to ṭā' and the wāw to yā'.
